audioscript.text: You will hear a woman asking a friend for restaurant recommendations.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4.

audioscript.text: I've been meaning to ask you for some advice about restaurants.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I need to book somewhere to celebrate my sister's 30th birthday, and I like the sound of that place you went to for your mum's 50th.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: The Junction?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yeah, I'd definitely recommend that for a special occasion.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: We had a great time there.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Everyone really enjoyed it.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Where is it again?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I can't remember.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: It's on Greyson Street, only about a 2 minute walk from the station.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Oh, that's good.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I'd prefer not to have to drive anywhere, but I don't want to have to walk too far either.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes, the location is perfect, but that's not necessarily why I'd recommend it.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: The food's amazing. If you like fish,
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: it's probably the best restaurant in town for that.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says The Junction is *'probably the best restaurant in town for that'* — and *'that'* refers back to *'fish'* from the previous sentence. So the answer is **fish**.

audioscript.text: It's always really fresh, and there are lots of interesting dishes to choose from, but all the food is good there.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Is it really expensive?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: It's certainly not cheap, but for a special occasion, I think it's fine.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's got a great atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: And before dinner, you can go up on the roof and have a drink.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says *'before dinner, you can go up on the roof and have a drink'* — this directly tells you where to go for a drink. So the answer is **roof**.

audioscript.text: It's really nice up there, but you need to book.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's very popular, as the views are spectacular.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Hmm, sounds good.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: So that's definitely a possibility then.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Is there anywhere else you can think of?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: um If you want somewhere a bit less formal then you could try Paloma.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Where's that?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I haven't heard of it.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, it's quite new.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's only been open a few months, but it's got a great reputation already.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's in a really beautiful old building on Bow Street.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Oh, I think I know where you mean.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Right beside the cinema.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes, that's it.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I've only been there a couple of times, but I was really impressed.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: The chef used to work at Don Filipe's apparently.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I was really sorry when that closed down.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: So is all the food they serve Spanish then?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yeah, you can get lots of small dishes to share, which always works really well if you're in a group.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q3: The woman asks if all the food is *'Spanish'*, and the friend confirms by saying *'Yeah, you can get lots of small dishes to share'* — this connects **Spanish** food to sharing. So the answer is **Spanish**.

audioscript.text: Hmm.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Worth thinking about.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yeah, there's a lively atmosphere, and the waiters are really friendly.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: The only thing is that you need to pay a 50 pound deposit to book a table.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: A lot of restaurants are doing that these days.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: I should have a look at the menu to check there's a good choice of vegetarian dishes.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: A couple of my friends have stopped eating meat.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Not sure, I'd say the selection of those would be quite limited.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q4: The woman worries about a *'good choice of vegetarian dishes'*, and the friend replies the selection of *'those'* would be *'quite limited'* — **'those'** means **vegetarian** dishes. So the answer is **vegetarian**.

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: I've just thought of another idea.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Have you been to the Audley?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: No, don't think I've heard of it.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: How's it spelt?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: AUDLEY.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q5: The friend spells the restaurant name clearly as *'AUDLEY'* when asked. So the answer is **Audley**.

audioscript.text: You must have heard of it.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: There's been a lot about it in the press.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I don't tend to pay much attention to that kind of thing.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: So where is it exactly?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: It's in that hotel near Baxter Bridge, on the top floor.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says *'It's in that hotel near Baxter Bridge, on the top floor'* — this tells you the restaurant is at the top of a **hotel**. So the answer is **hotel**.

audioscript.text: Oh, the views would be incredible from up there.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yeah, I'd love to go.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I can't think of the chef's name, but she was a judge on that TV cookery show recently, and she's written a couple of cookery books.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Oh, Angela Frayn.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: That's the one.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Anyway, it's had excellent reviews from all the newspapers.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage says *'it's had excellent reviews from all the newspapers'* — this means all the **reviews** are very good. So the answer is **reviews**.

audioscript.text: That would be a memorable place for a celebration.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Definitely, obviously it's worth going there just for the view, but the food is supposed to be really special.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: She only likes cooking with local products, doesn't she?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Everything at the restaurant has to be sourced within a short distance, and absolutely nothing flown in from abroad.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says everything must be *'sourced within a short distance'* and nothing *'flown in from abroad'* — this means she only uses **local** ingredients. So the answer is **local**.

audioscript.text: I imagine it's really expensive though.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Well, you could go for the set lunch.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That's quite reasonable for a top class restaurant, £30 a head.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says the set lunch is *'£30 a head'* — **'a head'** means per person. So the answer is **30** or **thirty**.

audioscript.text: In the evening, I think it would be more like £50.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: At least that I should think, but I'm sure everyone would enjoy it.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: It's not the kind of place you leave feeling hungry though, is it?
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: With tiny portions.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: No, the reviews I've read didn't mention that.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I imagine they'd be average.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q10: When asked if portions are tiny, the friend says *'I imagine they'd be average'* — this directly describes the portion size. So the answer is **average**.

audioscript.text: Well, that's all great.
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: Thanks...
audioscript.speaker: WOMAN

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.

test_text.title: Introduction to Pottery at Edelman Pottery

audioscript.text: Part 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a potter, Heather McCallum speaking to a group of people who are visiting a pottery, a place where people make pots and other objects from clay.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, and welcome.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: My name's Heather McCallum, and I'm one of the potters who work here at Edelman Pottery.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: Before we go into the workshop, I just want to say a bit about the craft of pottery.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: Then we'll have a look at the equipment, and you can try making a pot of your own.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: Like many people, I'm sure you know that pottery as an art form is tens of thousands of years old, and we know this because it stands the test of time.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says pottery *'stands the test of time'* and that baskets and pictures *'don't survive in the earth in the same way that pots do'*. This means pottery **lasts longer** in the ground than other art forms. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Things like baskets and pictures don't survive in the earth in the same way that pots do.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says pottery *'stands the test of time'* and that baskets and pictures *'don't survive in the earth in the same way that pots do'*. This means pottery **lasts longer** in the ground than other art forms. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And even if ancient pots are found in small pieces, they still provide a lot of information about the past.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: There's no doubt that pottery has given archaeologists a fascinating insight into how ancient humans lived.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: The shape of an artifact may have been lost.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: But archaeologists can tell whether the pots were for, say, storage or cooking by examining the impressions on the clay, the scratches from tools.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says archaeologists tell the use of pots by *'examining the impressions on the clay, the scratches from tools'*. **'Impressions'** and **'scratches'** are **'marks'** on the pot. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: And the clay itself can reveal where the pots came from.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: When I ask people why they want to take a pottery class with me, they sometimes talk about these things, like our ancestors.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: They hope that something they create will also last longer than they do.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says some people hope their creation *'will also last longer than they do'*. **'Last longer than they do'** means the item will **outlive them**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: That their work, whether it is good or not, might say something about humanity many years after their death.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: Of course, you will all have your own reasons for coming here.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: As far as I'm concerned, what I love most is the concentration you need to make a good pot.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q14: Heather says what she loves most is the *'concentration'* needed, and that *'focus takes you away from the stresses of everyday life'*. Taking away stress is a **calming effect**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: That focus takes you away from the stresses of everyday life.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q14: Heather says what she loves most is the *'concentration'* needed, and that *'focus takes you away from the stresses of everyday life'*. Taking away stress is a **calming effect**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: If you're elderly, it's also good exercise for hands and wrists.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: And helps with arthritis, and of course, it's a fun activity for children, because it's so messy.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: Here at Edelman Pottery we show you some of the basic pottery techniques, so that you can use these to create whatever you wish, a gift for a friend perhaps, like nearly everyone who comes here.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: I'm sure this is the first time you will have tried the art, so we'll keep things simple today.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q15: Heather says *'I'm sure this is the first time you will have tried the art'*. **'First time'** means they have **never made a pot before**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Now, before we move on, can I just say a word about what you're wearing?
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM

audioscript.text: As we said in our email, please remove any watches, necklaces, et cetera.
audioscript.speaker: HEATHER MCCALLUM
audioscript.explain: Q16: Heather says *'please remove any watches, necklaces, et cetera'*. **'Remove'** means **'take off'**, and watches and necklaces are **'jewellery'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: You will hear part of a presentation by an urban planning student about the role of rivers in cities around the world.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: It's quite hard to think of a city that doesn't have a big river running through it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If you think about the major cities in the world, Shanghai, New York, Mumbai, London, they're nearly all built on rivers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When these cities were established hundreds or even thousands of years ago, the rivers were a big part of people's lives.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 16th century London, the quickest way to get from one part of the city to another was by river.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But people also used the river for fishing, as the water then was relatively clean.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And they would also go on boat trips up and down the river just for pleasure, as a relaxing escape from the noise and bustle of the city streets.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But as industries developed and populations increased city rivers suffered.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The rising number of people meant there was a huge increase in the amount of sewage discharged into the rivers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Rivers had always been used for this purpose.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But when the number of inhabitants was so small, that wasn't such a problem.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, as cities grew to over a million inhabitants, the impact on the rivers became more serious.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In addition, other types of pollution increased as factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The question asks about pollution from something on the river bank. The passage says *'factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water'* — **'beside the river'** means on the river bank. So the answer is **factories**.

audioscript.text: This got worse over time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As recently as 1957, scientists at London's Natural History Museum declared that the River Thames was dead, in biological terms.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The question says the River Thames was declared biologically something. The passage directly states scientists *'declared that the River Thames was dead, in biological terms'*. So the answer is **dead**.

audioscript.text: As the water was too filthy to support any kind of life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But in recent years, as rivers lost their industrial function, cities have begun to recognize their true value, and to take steps to clean them up.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, the River Thames is now cleaner than it's been for 150 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These days you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale, which had got lost and swam up the river from the sea by mistake.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The question mentions seals and even a something have been seen. The passage says *'you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale'*. So the answer is **whale**.

audioscript.text: Unfortunately they didn't succeed, but the problem was disorientation rather than the quality of the water.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then, all around the world Riverside areas are now seen as prime sites for development.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Warehouses that were once used for storing goods are now being converted into expensive restaurants, and also into apartments with river views, which are in great demand and sell for astronomical prices.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The question says warehouses are converted to restaurants and something. The passage says warehouses are *'being converted into expensive restaurants, and also into apartments with river views'*. So the answer is **apartments**.

audioscript.text: In Los Angeles on the west coast of the USA, an architect has plans to revitalize the banks of the river.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And to make a park there, which can provide facilities for sports, as well as a natural environment for relaxing in.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The question asks about plans to build a riverside something in Los Angeles. The passage says an architect has plans *'to make a park there'* by the river. So the answer is **park**.

audioscript.text: It's also hoped that the Riverside can be used for other purposes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's been proposed that facilities could be provided for displaying projects related to various kinds of art that have been produced by local people, for example.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The question asks about displaying something projects. The passage says facilities could be provided for *'displaying projects related to various kinds of art'*. So the answer is **art**.

audioscript.text: In the city of Paris, during the summer months of July and August, all the traffic is banned from the roads by the sides of the river, and the banks are transformed into beaches where people can relax in deck chairs under potted palm trees, sunbathe, or buy a drink or a snack while enjoying the view.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The question asks what is created on the sides of the river in Paris every summer. The passage says the banks are *'transformed into beaches'* during July and August. So the answer is **beaches**.

audioscript.text: But to make the most of our rivers in our increasingly crowded cities, we need to allow them to regain their original purpose, and be used as a means of transport.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Reclaiming our streets from cars and lorries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To do this, we'll have to shift more traffic back to the river, but this time cleanly and silently.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Making the most of modern technology.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Already, more than 2 billion passengers use the ferry to travel in cities around the world, like Istanbul, San Francisco, and New York.

audioscript.text: And in future, the final stage could even be carried out by drone, although at present this isn't allowed.

utterances.text: In 16th century London, the quickest way to get from one part of the city to another was by river.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But people also used the river for fishing, as the water then was relatively clean.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And they would also go on boat trips up and down the river just for pleasure, as a relaxing escape from the noise and bustle of the city streets.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But as industries developed and populations increased city rivers suffered.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The rising number of people meant there was a huge increase in the amount of sewage discharged into the rivers.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Rivers had always been used for this purpose.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But when the number of inhabitants was so small, that wasn't such a problem.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: However, as cities grew to over a million inhabitants, the impact on the rivers became more serious.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: In addition, other types of pollution increased as factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q31: The question asks about pollution from something on the river bank. The passage says *'factories were built beside the river and discharged their waste materials into the water'* — **'beside the river'** means on the river bank. So the answer is **factories**.

utterances.text: This got worse over time.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: As recently as 1957, scientists at London's Natural History Museum declared that the River Thames was dead, in biological terms.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The question says the River Thames was declared biologically something. The passage directly states scientists *'declared that the River Thames was dead, in biological terms'*. So the answer is **dead**.

utterances.text: As the water was too filthy to support any kind of life.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But in recent years, as rivers lost their industrial function, cities have begun to recognize their true value, and to take steps to clean them up.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For example, the River Thames is now cleaner than it's been for 150 years.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: These days you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale, which had got lost and swam up the river from the sea by mistake.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q33: The question mentions seals and even a something have been seen. The passage says *'you can see seals swimming in the water, and recently people had to try to rescue a whale'*. So the answer is **whale**.

utterances.text: Unfortunately they didn't succeed, but the problem was disorientation rather than the quality of the water.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Then, all around the world Riverside areas are now seen as prime sites for development.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Warehouses that were once used for storing goods are now being converted into expensive restaurants, and also into apartments with river views, which are in great demand and sell for astronomical prices.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q34: The question says warehouses are converted to restaurants and something. The passage says warehouses are *'being converted into expensive restaurants, and also into apartments with river views'*. So the answer is **apartments**.

utterances.text: In Los Angeles on the west coast of the USA, an architect has plans to revitalize the banks of the river.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And to make a park there, which can provide facilities for sports, as well as a natural environment for relaxing in.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q35: The question asks about plans to build a riverside something in Los Angeles. The passage says an architect has plans *'to make a park there'* by the river. So the answer is **park**.

utterances.text: It's also hoped that the Riverside can be used for other purposes.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It's been proposed that facilities could be provided for displaying projects related to various kinds of art that have been produced by local people, for example.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q36: The question asks about displaying something projects. The passage says facilities could be provided for *'displaying projects related to various kinds of art'*. So the answer is **art**.

utterances.text: In the city of Paris, during the summer months of July and August, all the traffic is banned from the roads by the sides of the river, and the banks are transformed into beaches where people can relax in deck chairs under potted palm trees, sunbathe, or buy a drink or a snack while enjoying the view.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q37: The question asks what is created on the sides of the river in Paris every summer. The passage says the banks are *'transformed into beaches'* during July and August. So the answer is **beaches**.

utterances.text: But to make the most of our rivers in our increasingly crowded cities, we need to allow them to regain their original purpose, and be used as a means of transport.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Reclaiming our streets from cars and lorries.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: To do this, we'll have to shift more traffic back to the river, but this time cleanly and silently.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Making the most of modern technology.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Already, more than 2 billion passengers use the ferry to travel in cities around the world, like Istanbul, San Francisco, and New York.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q38: The question says over 2 billion passengers travel by something. The passage says *'more than 2 billion passengers use the ferry to travel'*. So the answer is **ferry**.

utterances.text: And these numbers are set to rise further, admittedly it's not a fast way of traveling, but neither is a car when it's stuck in traffic.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Of course, passenger traffic on roads might decrease as more people start working from home.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But another recent development, the huge rise in online shopping, has meant that another form of urban traffic just keeps on growing, and that's deliveries.

utterances.text: One freight barge can replace 44 large trucks, uses far less energy, and causes less pollution.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: When the barge docks at the Riverside the parcels could be taken the last few kilometers to their final destination on cargo bikes, electric ones of course.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This is already happening in the Dutch city of Amsterdam.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And in future, the final stage could even be carried out by drone, although at present this isn't allowed.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q40: The question says in future, goods could be transported by something. The passage says the final stage *'could even be carried out by drone'*. So the answer is **drone**.

utterances.text: Wouldn't it be great to unblock our city centers in this way?
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Looking further ahead...

audioscript.text: Part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman who is caring for her elderly mother talking to a friend.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: It's really good to see you, Tom.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Since I had to give up work, I feel I'm losing touch with my friends and colleagues.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: We really miss you in the office.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: We were all so sorry you had to leave.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: But you must be relieved to have more time to look after your mother.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: How is she?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Well, she's very cheerful, but she needs a lot of help.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Have you tried to get any support from the local council?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: No, I didn't know I could.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Yes, they offer different kinds of practical support.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: They realize that carers sometimes need time for all the other responsibilities they have apart from the person they're caring for, and also that they sometimes need a break.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says carers *'sometimes need a break'* — the question asks what the carer gets, and **'a break'** is exactly what is offered. So the answer is **break**.

audioscript.text: uh Absolutely.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Ok, so tell me more.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: How do I go about getting this support?
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Well, you'd have to have an assessment of your mother's needs.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: That means someone would come round and talk to you about the situation and what you need.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: So for a start, they'd want to know the amount of time you spend looking after your mother every day.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says *'they'd want to know the amount of time you spend looking after your mother'* — **'amount of time'** means **'how much time'**. So the answer is **time**.

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Then they'll probably ask you what sorts of tasks you do for your mother during the day.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Things like if she needs help with getting dressed, for example.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Right, I help her with that, and also I help her get into the shower in the morning.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL
audioscript.explain: Q3: The woman says *'I help her get into the shower in the morning'* — **'help her get into the shower'** means **'helping her have a shower'**. So the answer is **shower**.

audioscript.text: Yes, that sort of thing.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: They'll probably ask you if you do the shopping for her, and help her at meal times, and whether she can cope using money.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage asks *'whether she can cope using money'* — **'cope using money'** means **'dealing with money'**. So the answer is **money**.

audioscript.text: Yes, that's becoming a bit of a problem.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: She used to be very good at it, but uh not anymore.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: And be ready to tell them about anything you find particularly difficult about caring for your mother.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: So recently, I've noticed she started to have quite bad problems with her memory.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL
audioscript.explain: Q5: The woman says her mother has *'quite bad problems with her memory'* — **'problems with her memory'** means **'loss of memory'**. So the answer is **memory**.

audioscript.text: If I wasn't there, I think she'd forget to eat for example, and often she doesn't seem quite sure what day it is.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Yes, tell them about that.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And are there any physical difficulties you have caring for her?
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Lifting her for example?
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q6: The friend asks about *'physical difficulties'* and gives an example: *'Lifting her for example?'* — this is the difficult task. So the answer is **lifting**.

audioscript.text: Yes, she's quite heavy, and I'm afraid of hurting my back.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: I'd be in real trouble if that happened.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: They can give you advice about that, and also about how to avoid the possibility of your mom having a fall.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage talks about *'how to avoid the possibility of your mom having a fall'* — **'avoid'** means **'prevent'**, and **'having a fall'** is **'a fall'**. So the answer is **fall**.

audioscript.text: Great.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: So once they've done this assessment, if I'm eligible, uh what happens next?
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Well, they might support you financially, so they might help you with transport costs, like if you have to get a taxi to take your mother for an appointment for example.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage gives an example of transport costs: *'if you have to get a taxi'* — **'get a taxi'** means the **'cost of a taxi'**. So the answer is **taxi**.

audioscript.text: I usually drive her myself, actually.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: So could I claim for the petrol?
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: You could, and you can claim for the insurance too.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says *'you can claim for the insurance too'* — **'insurance'** is a car-related cost, just like fuel. So the answer is **insurance**.

audioscript.text: Oh, right.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: And if you need help with the housework, they can arrange for someone to come along once or twice a week.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: And one other thing, I hope you don't mind me saying this, but it's important you look after yourself, and it seems to me you're under quite a bit of stress.
audioscript.speaker: TOM
audioscript.explain: Q10: The friend says *'you're under quite a bit of stress'* and the council can give advice on *'how to minimize it'* — **'minimize'** means **'reduce'**, and **'it'** refers to **'stress'**. So the answer is **stress**.

audioscript.text: I am, yes.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Well tell the council, because they may be able to give you some advice on how to minimize it.
audioscript.speaker: TOM

audioscript.text: Really?
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Though, actually, I feel so much better having talked to you.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: I'll get in touch with the council straight away.
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: Now, shall we go for coffee or some?
audioscript.speaker: CAROL

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a man who works for Elmleigh Town Council talking to some people who want to join the small town's volunteer scheme.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: I'm Steve Wainwright from Elmleigh Town Council, and I organize the town's volunteer scheme.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: I'm delighted you're all interested in joining the scheme.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: Our volunteers help to create a sense of community among the many people who live in our historic town of Elmleigh, and make residents and visitors feel welcome at local events.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: At first, I'll mention just a few of the activities that volunteers carry out.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: One is to walk around the town center streets wearing our volunteer T-shirt.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: Tourists often ask how to get to a particular shop, and they might also be grateful for recommendations about what to visit.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says volunteers walk around and tourists ask *'how to get to a particular shop'* and want *'recommendations about what to visit'* — this is **giving advice to visitors**. So the answer is **D**.

audioscript.text: The town holds a large number of concerts each year, and part of the volunteers' role is to get everyone in the audience to the right place as smoothly as possible.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says the volunteers' role is to *'get everyone in the audience to the right place'* because people *'head for the wrong section of the hall'* — this means **helping people find their seats**. So the answer is **I**.

audioscript.text: You'd be surprised how many people buy tickets then don't check them, and head for the wrong section of the hall.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says the volunteers' role is to *'get everyone in the audience to the right place'* because people *'head for the wrong section of the hall'* — this means **helping people find their seats**. So the answer is **I**.

audioscript.text: Volunteers may get involved with community groups.
audioscript.speaker: STEVE WAINWRIGHT

audioscript.text: Such as sports clubs or gardeners' associations, here the volunteers talk about how groups can help each other.

audioscript.text: Good morning.

audioscript.text: Hi, this is Shelley Mayer.

audioscript.text: I'm renting your house on Archwood Avenue.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: Oh yes, hello, Ms Mayer.

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I remember.

audioscript.text: That's right.

audioscript.text: I've recommended them to other people, and I've always heard positive reports about them.

audioscript.text: Could you give me an idea of their costs?

audioscript.text: It says the monthly price per room starts at $105 and goes up to $239.

audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Oh, I see.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: I probably won't need that.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: That's for both furniture and also electronic equipment.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: First of all, you have to take out insurance on the furniture, and you need to organize that yourself.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage says for Larch Furniture, *'you have to take out insurance on the furniture, and you need to organize that yourself'*. So you must have your own **insurance**.

audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: But I figure that might not be a problem for you.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: You're renting the house for 12 months after all, aren't you?
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: Yes. OK. Well, I...
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: Sorry to interrupt.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: I just thought of another furniture rental company.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: It's called Space Rentals, and it's located very near to the house.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says *'It's called Space Rentals'*. So the name of the company is **Space** Rentals.

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: I don't have any information about their charges.
audioscript.speaker: MAN

audioscript.text: So it's best to use their app to find out what it would cost you to use them.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says *'it's best to use their app to find out what it would cost you'*. So you see the **app** for the most up-to-date prices.

audioscript.text: OK, thanks.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: I'll do that.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: One good thing about that company is that if you don't like the furniture once it's delivered, you can request exchanges, as long as you do that within a week of receiving it.
audioscript.speaker: MAN
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says *'you can request exchanges, as long as you do that within a week of receiving it'*. **'Within a week'** means **'within 7 days'**, so **exchanges** are allowed.

audioscript.text: That sounds really great.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: Ok, well thanks very much, that's so helpful.
audioscript.speaker: SHELLEY MAYER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.

audioscript.text: Part 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear an archaeologist who is part of a community project to excavate an ancient village, talking to members of the public who are visiting the site.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, I'm Hayden.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: I'm one of the archaeologists investigating the site here at Bidcaster.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: This is the third summer for this community project.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: And most of the people digging here are volunteers.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: I'm a full-time archaeologist for the town council, but I was asked to join the project by NHA,
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says Hayden was asked to join the project by *'NHA, a charity which sets up projects like this up and down the country'*. So a **national charity** started the project, not the local council or castle owners. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: a charity which sets up projects like this up and down the country.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says Hayden was asked to join the project by *'NHA, a charity which sets up projects like this up and down the country'*. So a **national charity** started the project, not the local council or castle owners. The answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: As you can see, we're next to Bidcaster Castle, which is great, because the owners let us use their facilities.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: So, how did we get to where we are today?
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Many archaeology projects happen when an ancient object is found, and in our case that object was a gold coin.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Coins are often found by people using metal detectors to look for things buried in the ground, or coins are uncovered when wild animals like rabbits have been digging tunnels.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Here, a walker found it on the ground after a rainstorm washed away some of the earth and sand.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'a walker found it on the ground after a rainstorm washed away some of the earth and sand'*. **'Rainstorm washed away'** means **'heavy rain had removed'** the soil. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: When the story of the gold coin hit the news, Peter Swift, an amateur historian, contacted me to say he believed there had been a village on this site.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Centuries before the castle was built.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Just by chance, the team found some old maps and documents in our library, which showed 500-year-old drawings of ruined buildings on the grassy area between the outer stone walls of the castle and the river.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says the team found *'old maps and documents in our library'* which showed drawings of ruined buildings. **'Old maps and documents'** means **'old records'**, and finding them was a lucky discovery. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: We knew then we were onto something.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Over the three summers the team has been here, we found the remains of several buildings, and more broken pots than you can count.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Normally you'd expect to find brooches and other jewelry.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: But we're still waiting to uncover any such items.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says they are *'still waiting to uncover any such items'* — **'such items'** refers back to *'brooches and other jewelry'*. So they are still hoping to find **pieces of jewellery**. The answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: The people who once lived here were skilled at making tools from animal bones, as you'll see when you visit the exhibition.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: Besides the discovery of the village, we've also found evidence of human activity on the other side of the river.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: No other houses or huts so far.
audioscript.speaker: HAYDEN

audioscript.text: But we can see the borders of an ancient field system.

audioscript.text: You will hear two theater studies students, Maya and Finn, discussing their project on theater programs.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.

audioscript.text: So Finn, I've done as much as I can for our project on theater programs.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: How's your research coming along?
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Ok, Maya.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: I didn't know theater programs are called playbills in the USA, till I started looking into the topic.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Even though I struggled to find many useful websites, I'm glad we picked this subject.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: No one else on the course is doing the same as us, although it is one of the research areas of the module convenor.
audioscript.speaker: FINN
audioscript.explain: Q21: Finn says *'No one else on the course is doing the same as us'* — this means other students did **not** pick this topic. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: That might actually put some people off.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Huh, I suppose so.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Anyway, I hadn't realized there are actually companies specializing in creating theater programs.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Yes, they're quite common nowadays.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Contrary to what many people think, theatres don't hire people to do the programs.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q22: Maya says *'Contrary to what many people think, theatres don't hire people to do the programs'* — **'hire'** means **'pay'**. The mistaken belief is that theatres pay companies, so the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: In fact companies buy the rights to publish programs on the theatre's behalf.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q22: Maya says *'Contrary to what many people think, theatres don't hire people to do the programs'* — **'hire'** means **'pay'**. The mistaken belief is that theatres pay companies, so the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And then make their money selling advertising space within the program booklet.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: It must be easier for theaters to do it that way.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: I remember reading something about programs in early British theater.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: It said that the cast was always very important.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Yeah, audiences were very familiar with leading actors, and big names would draw huge crowds.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: But I hadn't realized that if the program named a famous actor, that's who the public expected to perform, and if that didn't happen, people accused the theater of breaking their agreement with the audience.
audioscript.speaker: FINN
audioscript.explain: Q23: Finn says if a program named a famous actor, people expected that actor, and if not, they *'accused the theater of breaking their agreement'* — an **'agreement'** is like a **'contract'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: They would demand refunds, and if they didn't get them, there were riots.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Outrageous. That'd never happen now.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: No, people are too polite, even when they're disappointed if the star of the show misses a performance.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: We should definitely include that information about early audiences in our project.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: I also think it's important to mention that lots of ordinary people at that time were illiterate, so theater programs were of limited value in advertising plays.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q24: Maya says programs were *'of limited value in advertising'* because people were illiterate, so actors *'parade around the streets'* to announce plays — this means they **promoted** their own plays. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: When a company of actors arrived in a town, they'd parade around the streets in their costumes, beating drums and announcing their upcoming performances.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q24: Maya says programs were *'of limited value in advertising'* because people were illiterate, so actors *'parade around the streets'* to announce plays — this means they **promoted** their own plays. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Interesting.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: I couldn't imagine that happening now either.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Hmm.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: There's also an interesting comparison to make between 18th and 19th century programs.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Wasn't it in the 19th century that theater programs started to resemble programs today?
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: And unlike programs from the 18th century, they always used color.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: And there was a greater variety of designs. But personally, I think 18th-century programs were superior, because they told the theater goers so many things, including about the actors.
audioscript.speaker: FINN
audioscript.explain: Q25: Finn says 18th-century programs *'told the theater goers so many things'* like actors, writer, and plot — **'told so many things'** means they were **more informative**. Maya agrees, so the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: And about the writer, the plot, and sometimes the history of the play.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q25: Finn says 18th-century programs *'told the theater goers so many things'* like actors, writer, and plot — **'told so many things'** means they were **more informative**. Maya agrees, so the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: What should we say about theater programs in the 20th century?
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: I reckon the most important thing is the dramatic change they underwent during World War 2.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: When the government imposed restrictions on the use of paper.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Yeah, but that was only in the UK, in the USA, programs or rather playbills continued to be published in the same format.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Well, here in the UK, programs became merely a single sheet of paper folded to create 4 pages for text.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Hmm.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: What I don't really get is that after the war, they didn't go back to being more than one sheet, or change in any way for over 25 years.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA
audioscript.explain: Q26: Maya says she doesn't get why after the war, programs *'didn't go back to being more than one sheet, or change in any way for over 25 years'* — this means British programs **failed to develop** for a long time. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: I know there were paper shortages after the war, but only for 5 or 10 years.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.text: Hmm, strange.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: I thought this was a good program to show, not because of the pictures.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: But because it contains articles written by members of the theater company, so we can learn how the production was created, and the thoughts and feelings of the cast.
audioscript.speaker: FINN

audioscript.text: Good.

audioscript.text: I've got a copy of a program that's now in a museum.
audioscript.speaker: MAYA

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: It's only relatively recently that designers have become aware of the need to be inclusive when designing products, but what does that mean exactly?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, it simply means designing products that span economic, social and cultural barriers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It means making sure products are accessible.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So that as many different types of people as possible can use them without any type of adaptation having to be made to the original design.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says products should be used *'without any type of adaptation having to be made'* — **'adaptation'** means a change or adjustment. So the answer is **adaptation**.

audioscript.text: Inclusive design is often linked with universal design, although they are not quite the same thing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Universal design aims to make products that work for everyone.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And that includes considering the needs of people who have cognitive difficulties, which can present quite a challenge.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says universal design includes *'people who have cognitive difficulties'* — **'difficulties'** here means **'problems'**. So the answer is **cognitive**.

audioscript.text: Today, examples of successful inclusive design can be seen all around us.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In workplaces, it is common to see desks which can be adjusted to suit people of different heights, or for wheelchair users.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'desks which can be adjusted'* help avoid *'back or neck problems'* — **'adjusted'** means they can be changed to fit different people. So the answer is **Desks**.

audioscript.text: This still isn't always the case, however, and is one reason why office workers often suffer from back or neck problems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'desks which can be adjusted'* help avoid *'back or neck problems'* — **'adjusted'** means they can be changed to fit different people. So the answer is **Desks**.

audioscript.text: You'll find another example in the public toilets of countless hotels, airports and offices.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Taps that you activate by sensor require no pressing or twisting movements.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'Taps that you activate by sensor'* are in public toilets and are *'easier for people'* to use — **'easier'** means less difficult. So the answer is **Taps**.

audioscript.text: These are not only more hygienic, they're also easier for people with dexterity or mobility issues.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'Taps that you activate by sensor'* are in public toilets and are *'easier for people'* to use — **'easier'** means less difficult. So the answer is **Taps**.

audioscript.text: The tech industry has been criticized in the past for focusing too much on young consumers, but this is changing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Many products are now designed with the elderly in mind.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, it's well known that vision declines with age, and that we also become worse at distinguishing between similar colors.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In particular shades of blue, which is why software designers rarely create interfaces with this color.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says older people struggle with *'shades of blue'*, so designers *'rarely create interfaces with this color'* — **'rarely'** means they avoid it. So the answer is **blue**.

audioscript.text: Motor skills also decline with age.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And some people have difficulty doing everyday things, like picking up a cup or opening a door.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This can also affect their ability to use a mouse or keyboard.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So voice access is now a routine way of making commands.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says *'voice access is now a routine way of making commands'* — **'voice'** is using your speech instead of hands. So the answer is **voice**.

audioscript.text: It's worth looking at the problems non-inclusive designs cause when not enough consideration is given to a range of users, as it can have a serious impact on people's lives.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Access is one obvious example, because it has such a huge impact on disabled people's independence.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Not being able to access public transport because buses or trains are not wheelchair-friendly means many disabled people can't go out, unless someone goes with them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Safety is another issue, inexplicably, most cars are still crash tested using a dummy based on an average sized male.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This has safety implications for all women, particularly those who are pregnant, as the seat belts worn by the dummy are not adapted to accommodate them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says seatbelts are not adapted for *'those who are pregnant'* — **'those'** refers to women. So the answer is **pregnant**.

audioscript.text: Over the past 100 years, workplaces in the UK have on the whole become considerably safer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Employers are legally required to provide well maintained personal protective equipment or PPE.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Anything from goggles to full body suits, to workers who need it free of charge.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But most PPE is designed to fit men.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A recent report found that employers often think that when it comes to female workers, all they need to do to comply with this legal requirement is to buy jackets for example designed for a small man.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The problem with this is that women can be tall and still have much smaller shoulders than the average man.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says women *'have much smaller shoulders than the average man'* — this makes PPE jackets a bad fit. So the answer is **shoulders**.

audioscript.text: Ill-fitting PPE such as hi-vis jackets vests and body armor can put women at risk.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The report found that 95% of women said that their PPE often hampered their work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And that this problem was worst in the emergency services, particularly the police.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says the PPE problem is *'worst in the emergency services, particularly the police'* — **'particularly'** means especially. So the answer is **police**.

audioscript.text: Another problem is related to comfort at work.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A very common scenario in offices in summertime is to see women wrapped in blankets or wearing sweaters while the air conditioning is on high.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Meanwhile the men are in shorts and t-shirts.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is due to differences in metabolic rates for men and women.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There is a standard setting for air conditioning to be at a temperature of 21 degrees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says air conditioning is set to *'a temperature of 21 degrees'* and designed for men, making offices too cold for women — **'too low'** means the **temperature** is not warm enough. So the answer is **temperature**.

audioscript.text: Designed to suit men, and in most modern offices, it's not possible to turn the air conditioning up or down.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says air conditioning is set to *'a temperature of 21 degrees'* and designed for men, making offices too cold for women — **'too low'** means the **temperature** is not warm enough. So the answer is **temperature**.

audioscript.text: This means that many offices which mainly employ women are wasting energy by having the air conditioning set too high.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As you can see from the examples I've just mentioned, there are serious consequences for designs which don't consider the needs of all users.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is that is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about the impact of birds of prey on a farming community in Africa.

audioscript.text: We've been looking at different types of conflicts that may arise between wildlife and humans at the boundaries of protected areas, such as national parks and animal sanctuaries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'd like to illustrate this by telling you about some research that I've been involved in recently, in the Central African country of Zambia, in the area around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which contains over 300 of the listed birds of Zambia.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These include a number of birds of prey such as eagles, hawks and owls that live by hunting and killing other birds and animals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Now, most of the people living in the local communities near to the bird sanctuary are small scale farmers, and these birds of prey provide important social and ecological benefits to them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, a lot of damage can be caused to farmers' crops by rodents such as rats, which would consume the crops as they grow in the fields, as well as after harvesting, if they weren't hunted and killed by the birds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says birds hunt and kill *'rodents such as rats'* — **'rodents'** is the group, and **'rats'** is the specific example. The question asks what they destroy, so the answer is **rats**.

audioscript.text: And the predatory habits of these birds also protect farmers in other ways.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: uh For example, a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal'* — **'rural workers'** means **'farmers'**. So the birds prevent farmers from being bitten by **snakes**.

audioscript.text: And birds of prey have a major role in keeping their populations under control.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Local people have always been aware of these benefits, and for years even before the sanctuary was opened in 1973, the birds played a key role in the culture of the region.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, more recently the sanctuary and its birds have also become increasingly important to the community in economic terms, because at present, after a relatively slow start.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Tourism has become an important source of revenue for them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'Tourism has become an important source of revenue for them'* — **'revenue'** means **'income'** or **'economic support'**. So the birds encourage **tourism** in the area.

audioscript.text: However, although these birds of prey are protected by the government, their numbers are falling.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Some of these deaths are accidental.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Fatalities occur when birds alight on roads to catch and eat their prey, and are hit by fast-moving traffic.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says birds are *'hit by fast-moving traffic'* when they land on roads to hunt or sleep. So they are accidentally killed by **traffic**.

audioscript.text: Drivers in Zambia have to take special care at night, as birds may regard the quieter roads as safe places to sleep.

audioscript.text: Accidental deaths may also occur if these birds fly close to high voltage power lines, as they may be electrocuted.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is a particular danger in the heavy rain which can occur in the region in the months from December to April.

audioscript.text: As well as growing crops, small scale farmers in the area also rear chickens.

audioscript.text: These provide food for the farmer's families, as well as being an important source of income.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But they're also an easy target for birds of prey.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And so farmers may shoot these birds, which is illegal but understandable, or they may poison the birds, which again is illegal and can have negative effects on the ecosystem.

audioscript.text: So how else can farmers protect their chickens from birds of prey?

audioscript.text: Some people believe that to prevent the predators from settling near the area where the chickens are kept.

audioscript.text: It's best to keep this area free from vegetation, but in fact this is counterproductive, as it means the chickens have no cover to hide in.

utterances.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about the impact of birds of prey on a farming community in Africa.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
utterances.speaker: ANNOUNCER

utterances.text: We've been looking at different types of conflicts that may arise between wildlife and humans at the boundaries of protected areas, such as national parks and animal sanctuaries.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: I'd like to illustrate this by telling you about some research that I've been involved in recently, in the Central African country of Zambia, in the area around the Chembe Bird Sanctuary.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Which contains over 300 of the listed birds of Zambia.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: These include a number of birds of prey such as eagles, hawks and owls that live by hunting and killing other birds and animals.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Now, most of the people living in the local communities near to the bird sanctuary are small scale farmers, and these birds of prey provide important social and ecological benefits to them.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For example, a lot of damage can be caused to farmers' crops by rodents such as rats, which would consume the crops as they grow in the fields, as well as after harvesting, if they weren't hunted and killed by the birds.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q31: The passage says birds hunt and kill *'rodents such as rats'* — **'rodents'** is the group, and **'rats'** is the specific example. The question asks what they destroy, so the answer is **rats**.

utterances.text: And the predatory habits of these birds also protect farmers in other ways.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: uh For example, a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The passage says *'a major danger to rural workers is snakes, whose bite may be dangerous or even fatal'* — **'rural workers'** means **'farmers'**. So the birds prevent farmers from being bitten by **snakes**.

utterances.text: And birds of prey have a major role in keeping their populations under control.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Local people have always been aware of these benefits, and for years even before the sanctuary was opened in 1973, the birds played a key role in the culture of the region.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: However, more recently the sanctuary and its birds have also become increasingly important to the community in economic terms, because at present, after a relatively slow start.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Tourism has become an important source of revenue for them.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q33: The passage says *'Tourism has become an important source of revenue for them'* — **'revenue'** means **'income'** or **'economic support'**. So the birds encourage **tourism** in the area.

utterances.text: However, although these birds of prey are protected by the government, their numbers are falling.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Some of these deaths are accidental.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Fatalities occur when birds alight on roads to catch and eat their prey, and are hit by fast-moving traffic.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q34: The passage says birds are *'hit by fast-moving traffic'* when they land on roads to hunt or sleep. So they are accidentally killed by **traffic**.

utterances.text: Drivers in Zambia have to take special care at night, as birds may regard the quieter roads as safe places to sleep.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Accidental deaths may also occur if these birds fly close to high voltage power lines, as they may be electrocuted.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This is a particular danger in the heavy rain which can occur in the region in the months from December to April.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q35: The passage says electrocution is *'a particular danger in the heavy rain'* — **'heavy rain'** means a lot of **rain**. So the danger is greater when there is a lot of **rain**.

utterances.text: And local farmers also pose a threat to these birds.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: As well as growing crops, small scale farmers in the area also rear chickens.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: These provide food for the farmer's families, as well as being an important source of income.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But they're also an easy target for birds of prey.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And so farmers may shoot these birds, which is illegal but understandable, or they may poison the birds, which again is illegal and can have negative effects on the ecosystem.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q36: The passage says farmers *'may shoot these birds... or they may poison the birds'* — both are illegal. The question already mentions **'shoot'**, so the other illegal method is **poison**.

utterances.text: So how else can farmers protect their chickens from birds of prey?
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Some people believe that to prevent the predators from settling near the area where the chickens are kept.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It's best to keep this area free from vegetation, but in fact this is counterproductive, as it means the chickens have no cover to hide in.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And they'll be easier for the birds to see.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Another possibility would be to prevent the chickens from going outside at all, and to keep them safe from predators inside a building.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q37: The passage says one idea is to keep chickens *'safe from predators inside a building'* — but this is too expensive. So providing a **building** is an expensive solution.

utterances.text: But this would cost far too much to be a practical solution.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Nearly all the farmers reported that they spent a lot of time and effort trying to frighten off the birds of prey without actually harming them.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Most of the farmers had at least one dog, and said this was a big help at scaring away the predators.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q38: The passage says *'Most of the farmers had at least one dog'* and it helped scare away predators. So keeping a **dog** is one way to frighten the birds.

utterances.text: Some of the farmers also reported that during the breeding season.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: When the chickens were particularly vulnerable, they encouraged their children to watch over the chickens, and to hit pans with a metal spoon, so that the resulting noise would succeed in driving away birds that were trying to seize the young chicks.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q39: The passage says children hit pans with a metal spoon so *'the resulting noise would succeed in driving away birds'* — **'noise'** is the sound that scares them. So making a **noise** is another method.

utterances.text: None of these methods was 100% effective, so as a result the village people told us that rather than just using one method.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: They were forced to use a combination for them to have any effect. And even so, these birds of prey remain a major threat to the chickens' survival and cause considerable economic loss to farmers.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q40: The passage says farmers *'were forced to use a combination for them to have any effect'* — **'combination'** means using several methods together. So a **combination** of methods is most effective.

utterances.text: So we looked at the possibility of a longer-term solution to...
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
